title: Microtransaction protocol for tool races and client hedging
body:
Executive summary:

This doc proposes a lightweight "microtransaction" protocol layered on top of the Hosted API streaming and tool-calling surfaces to address two recurring problems: (1) tool-execution races and double side-effects when client SDKs hedge or retry, and (2) client-side hedging/backpressure tradeoffs when low-latency results are critical but tool calls are slow or variable. The goal is a minimal server+SDK contract that enables idempotent, observable tool interactions with low overhead and good ergonomics for JS/Python SDKs and existing streaming frames.

Problem space:
- Many product flows call external tools (search, DB write, code-exec) from model output. Models may emit multiple candidate tool invocations in quick succession. Client SDKs and edge proxies may hedge requests (send parallel model or tool calls) to reduce latency, which risks duplicate tool execution and inconsistent state.
- Streaming responses complicate the problem: partial tokens may arrive while the client decides whether to make a tool call. Cancel/timeout/hedge decisions can leave in-flight tool calls ambiguous.
- Existing approaches (server-side dedupe with long-lived idempotency keys, or forcing single-call semantics) either add developer burden or reintroduce latency.

Goals:
- Provide a simple protocol for atomic microtransactions around individual tool calls so that duplicates are detected/deduped server-side with minimal coordination.
- Support hedging: allow clients to issue multiple speculative tool calls but ensure only one effectful commit occurs.
- Keep streaming ergonomics good: allow partial frames and progressive updates while preserving deterministic tool outcome semantics.
- Minimal SDK changes: a small ergonomic surface for JS/Python to opt into hedged calls, reconnect-safe checkpoints, and a simple callback style for committed results.

Non-goals:
- This is not a full distributed transaction system. We will not attempt two-phase commit across multiple heterogeneous tools.
- We are not changing tool provider APIs; tooling partners must implement a small idempotency/decorrelation interface, or the Redwood broker will offer a shim.

Proposal overview:
Introduce a microtransaction lifecycle around each tool invocation. The lifecycle consists of three logical phases expressed via streaming frames and request metadata: PREPARE, EXECUTE (optionally hedged), and COMMIT/ABORT. The server maintains a short-lived transaction record keyed by a client-provided tx_id combined with a server-assigned short token.

Key elements:
- tx_id (client-supplied): opaque UTF-8 string chosen by client SDK or developer (UUID recommended). Used for dedupe/trace and for client-side reconnection semantics.
- tx_token (server-issued): short, single-use token returned by broker on PREPARE (63-bit base62). Signed by the server to prevent forging.
- Frame markers in streaming: TX:PREPARE, TX:EXECUTE, TX:COMMIT, TX:ABORT, TX:RESULT (see spec below).
- Idempotency window: server maintains tx records for a conservative default (60s) after COMMIT to dedupe late hedged attempts; configurable per-customer.
- Hedging policy: clients may issue multiple parallel EXECUTE frames for the same tx_id; the broker races them and honors the first successful COMMIT. Other executions receive a cancellation/rollback signal.

API and wire-level spec (sketch):
- Incoming client request (non-streaming or streaming initial envelope) may include header X-TX-ID: <uuid> and X-TX-MODE: prepare-only|execute|hedge-allowed.
- Server responds to PREPARE step with a small frame containing tx_token and capabilities: {tx_token, allowed_tools, ttl_ms}. For streaming, this is a short event frame: "TX:PREPARE: tx_token=<token> ttl=60000".
- EXECUTE frames include the tool name, arguments, and tx_token header. Example streaming payload lines: "TX:EXECUTE tx_token=abc123 tool=web_search args={"q":"x"}".
- Broker behavior: on receipt of first successful tool response for a tx_id, broker emits TX:RESULT (tool output) followed by TX:COMMIT. Other hedged executions are told to abort; downstream tool shims are sent a CANCEL/ROLLBACK hook or allowed to roll back on best-effort.
- If no EXECUTE frames are present and the model completes without a commit, the transaction either auto-aborts after ttl or the client can call finalize endpoint.

Example streaming exchange (high-level):
Client -> Server: POST /generate (stream=true) headers: X-TX-ID: a1b2
Server -> Client (stream event): TX:PREPARE tx_token=Zp9a ttl=60000
Client -> Server: TX:EXECUTE tx_token=Zp9a tool=search args=... (client hedges: issues same EXECUTE to two tool endpoints via proxy)
Tool A -> Broker: success result R1
Broker -> Client: TX:RESULT tool=search tx_token=Zp9a payload=R1
Broker -> Client: TX:COMMIT tx_token=Zp9a winner=ToolA
Broker -> Tool B: (notify) abort/ignore - or send rollback hook if supported

SDK ergonomics (JS/Python patterns):
- Default mode: "safe". SDK generates tx_id per tool-call decision point. Developer code uses a helper: await client.toolCall(txId, toolSpec, {hedge: true}) which returns the committed result or throws if aborted.
- Streaming helper: client.on('tx_prepare', (meta) => { /* decide to execute */ }); client.execTool({txId, tool:, args:, hedge:true}) -> Promise resolves with committed output once COMMIT arrives.
- Reconnect semantics: SDK persists outstanding tx_ids in memory and optionally to localStorage (configurable). On reconnect, SDK re-sends PREPARE or re-subscribes to TX events until COMMIT/ABORT.

Implementation model options:
1) Broker-first (recommended v1): Redwood runtime acts as a broker and coordinates dedupe. Tools are called via the broker; external tool providers accept a short-lived tx_token for attribution. Pros: minimal changes for clients. Cons: broker executes tool requests (adds load, requires secure shims).
2) Provider-assisted: Tool providers implement idempotency using tx_token and a small HTTP hook for rollback. Pros: less broker load. Cons: requires partner integration.
3) Hybrid: broker offers shim plus an optional provider hook for rollback optimization.

Backpressure and hedging policy details:
- Hedging windows must be tuned per-tool type. For very fast tools (sub-50ms) hedging is rarely helpful; for high-variance tools (search, external APIs) hedging buys latency at the cost of extra calls.
- SDK exposes configuration: max_parallel_execs, hedge_delay_ms, backoff_on_failure. Default: max_parallel_execs=2, hedge_delay_ms=80ms.
- Broker exposes per-route sampling telemetry so product can tune defaults by workload.

Observability and metrics:
- New metrics to emit: tx_created_count, tx_committed_count, tx_aborted_count, tx_duplicate_attempts, tool_executions_per_tx (histogram), hedged_success_ratio, hedged_cost_overhead (tokens/calls).
- Traces: each tx should be traceable across model, broker, and tool spans via tx_id and tx_token. Include a compact audit log for each tx.

Compatibility and fallbacks:
- Backward compatibility: if client doesn't provide X-TX-ID, runtime behaves as today (single-call semantics).
- Feature flagging: microtransaction protocol gated by account-level feature flag. Default off for existing customers until opt-in.

Rollout plan:
- Phase 0: internal experiments in staging with simulated tool latencies. Integrate with local dev SDKs.
- Phase 1: opt-in beta for selected customers and internal teams (solutions-engineering). Monitor tx metrics and duplicates.
- Phase 2: broader rollout with per-customer defaults and conservative idempotency windows.
- Phase 3: GA with docs, SDK syntactic sugar, and optional provider integration guide.

Operational considerations:
- Security: tx_token must be signed; broker should validate tokens and reject forged EXECUTES. Short TTLs mitigate replay risk.
- Cost: hedging increases tool invocations. Provide tooling in Console to estimate hedging cost per route and per model (projected additional calls per 1k requests).
- Privacy/compliance: broker logs tool payloads briefly for dedupe — ensure retention polices and opt-out for regulated workloads.

Open questions and tradeoffs:
- What is the right default idempotency window? (60s vs 30s vs 10s)
- How do we expose rollback semantics to tool vendors that don't support reversibility? (best-effort rollback vs compensating actions)
- Should tx_token rotation be used to limit replay across longer client reconnections?
- API ergonomics: should we make hedging boolean or provide a higher-level latency SLA object?

Next steps / action items:
- Eng (serving-runtime + infra) spike on broker proof-of-concept (2wk). Owner: Arjun.
- SDK team to prototype API surface for JS + Python helpers and local reconnect persistence (3wk). Owner: Maya.
- Product to draft pricing guidance and console UI mocks for hedging cost visibility. Owner: Tomislav.
- Solutions eng to identify 3 beta customers with hedging use cases and coordinate opt-in. Owner: Priya.

Appendix: developer example (JS pseudocode)
// Developer-facing minimal example
const tx = await client.generate({stream: true});
client.on('tx_prepare', async (meta) => {
  if (shouldCallSearch(meta)) {
    // lib handles hedging under the hood and returns final committed result
    const result = await client.execTool({txId: meta.txId, tool: 'web_search', args:{q:'x'}, hedge:true});
    console.log('Committed result', result);
  }
});

Notes:
This is an early design sketch intended to capture tradeoffs and a pragmatic v1 for experiments. The protocol should be iterated after a short internal dogfood period.
